reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / ACR-EULAR
clinicalPearls: A large-vessel vasculitis affecting the aorta and its major branches, characteristically in young women under 40, often of Asian descent
An early systemic phase of malaise, fever, and arthralgia may precede a later occlusive phase with vascular symptoms
Classic signs include diminished or absent peripheral pulses, blood pressure asymmetry between limbs, vascular bruits, and limb claudication
Renovascular involvement is an important cause of secondary hypertension in young patients
Inflammatory markers are often raised but can be normal despite ongoing vascular damage
Cross-sectional vascular imaging (MR or CT angiography, PET) demonstrates wall thickening, stenoses, occlusions, and aneurysms
Blood pressure should be measured in the arm with the least affected artery, as readings can be falsely low with subclavian stenosis
Corticosteroids are first-line, with steroid-sparing immunosuppressants or biologics for relapsing disease, and revascularisation reserved for critical lesions once inflammation is controlled
reference.pathophysiology: Takayasu arteritis is a chronic granulomatous large-vessel vasculitis of unknown cause. Cell-mediated immunity drives infiltration of the arterial wall by T cells, macrophages, and giant cells, beginning in the adventitia and vasa vasorum and extending through the media. Chronic inflammation produces intimal proliferation, medial destruction, and fibrosis, leading to segmental stenosis, occlusion, aneurysm formation, and thrombosis of the aorta and its principal branches. The resulting reduced or absent blood flow causes the ischaemic and 'pulseless' clinical manifestations.
additionalDifferentials: Giant cell arteritis (large-vessel involvement in older patients)
additionalInvestigations: Bilateral limb blood pressures and pulse examination with auscultation for bruits
MR or CT angiography of the aorta and branches for wall thickening, stenosis, and aneurysm
FDG-PET to assess vascular wall inflammatory activity
Inflammatory markers (ESR and CRP) recognising they may be normal
Assessment for renovascular hypertension and end-organ ischaemia
redFlags: Cerebrovascular symptoms, visual loss, or syncope from carotid or vertebral artery involvement
Severe or refractory hypertension from renal artery stenosis with risk of end-organ damage
Aortic aneurysm with risk of dissection or rupture, or significant aortic regurgitation
Myocardial ischaemia from coronary ostial involvement
reference.prognosis: With early diagnosis and immunosuppression many patients do well, but relapses are common and progressive vascular damage can cause hypertension, ischaemic complications, and aneurysms. Long-term morbidity relates to arterial stenoses, aortic regurgitation, and cardiovascular events.
pitfalls: Missing the diagnosis in a young woman with nonspecific systemic symptoms before vascular signs appear
Relying on a single-arm blood pressure that is falsely low due to subclavian stenosis
Assuming normal inflammatory markers exclude active disease
Attempting revascularisation during active inflammation with high restenosis risk
Overlooking renovascular hypertension as a treatable cause of raised blood pressure
